utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All my meetings with the gentlemen took place in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move on to discuss the commission you describe after the Markale shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record this is in paragraphs 18 to 21 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your statement you claim that there were a mixed commission that investigated your firing positions on the 6th of February, 1994, a day after the shelling. Is it correct that the commission you describe was not formed and it did not carry out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. There was a commission and it did carry out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You did not know any of the names of the UNPROFOR members who took part in this commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know the names then because we were not entitled to ask for their names or record their names, even when they came to carry out regular inspection duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you do not know how many UNPROFOR members were part of this inspection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were five or six of them, plus the interpreters. But there weren't fewer than five, that's for sure, because their Toyota was full. It was a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you do not know the names of anyone from the VRS Main Staff who were part of this commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you do not know the names of anyone from the SRK command who were part of this commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you don't know the name of any representatives from the brigade command who took part in this commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the brigade command there was the late Mile Pajic, Captain First Class, and First Class Warrant Officer Jakovljevic, I think that his first name was Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go through a couple of things now with you -- well, are those the only names that you can recall that were possibly part of this commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember those who were from my own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record, this is in paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- you state: "On 5 February 1994, I think that it was in the afternoon, the brigade command informed us that this incident had occurred and that a mixed commission would come to the battalion on that day or the following day to carry out an on-site investigation." You say that the brigade command informed "us." Who were you with when you first learned of this incident? Was it Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that incident from Mr. Gengo because he conveyed that to me at the meeting in the morning on the 6th. We had a meeting and I was proposing where I should go on that day, and then he told me where I should go, that I should go with the commission that will come to tour the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. That wasn't exactly my question. This part of your statement appears to indicate that on the 5th of February, 1994, the brigade command informed "us." Who were you with when you were informed about this commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement, where it says "we," I meant the commander. So it was through him. It's not that they called me personally to tell me. They talked to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "the commander," are you referring to your battalion commander, Mr. Gengo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- I would like to clarify this matter. In your statement you said: "... the brigade command informed us ..." Does it mean that Mr. Gengo as the commander informed himself and you? So I'm really a little bit confused. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gengo knew, I mean, that he received this order and he told the brigade command about this when we met in the morning when this commission was supposed to be accompanied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The sentence then should read: The brigade commander, Gengo, informed me. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Informed me in the morning hours of the 6th. That is how it should read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to take a break now, Mr. Weber. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do I understand that you have shared the information about the origin of D - what was it? - 417?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D471, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We investigated about the provenance of this document and we found it among the documents of the Tribunal. It is admitted in Karadzic case under number D2510, and it was admitted in Galic case under number D1312.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we've done our own check, Your Honour, and I withdraw any objection to the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D471 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to inform the Chamber, I've informed the Defence that I'll be finishing shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And so -- for scheduling purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzida --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not understand what the witness said. It was off mike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you were far away from the microphone when you said something, Mr. Dzida. So if you could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a draft coming from up here. There is something blowing in my direction. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask Madam Registrar to take care that something is done about it. If it is bothering you too much --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Weber will continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30709, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzida, I'm just going to go through a couple of your statements about this commission from the past. I'm going to start with your statement in the Karadzic case. And, sir, since the -- there is not a translation available for this, please be patient with me. I'm going to read it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I'm going to be reading, for the record, from paragraphs 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your statement in the past case states: "With regard to the incident referred to as G8, I know the following: On 5 February 1994, I think it was in the afternoon, the brigade command informed us that that incident occurred and that a mixed commission would come to the battalion on that or the following day to carry out an on-site investigation." The beginning of the next paragraph states: "On 6 February 1994, between 0900 and 1000 hours, representatives of the GS /Main Staff/ of the VRS /Army of Republika Srpska/, the SRK /Sarajevo-Romanija Corps/, UNPROFOR, and the 1st Rpbr came," and then you continue to describe. Sir, does this accurately record, what I've read to you, your past statement from the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly. As far as I can remember, the commander appointed me in the morning at that meeting to be team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please go to page 10 of this same statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this same statement in the Karadzic case, you provided corrections in additional paragraphs to the statement, and you made corrections during your proofing in the Karadzic case on this same topic. In paragraph 29 you stated: "Two or three days after the Markale incident in February 1994, an UNPROFOR commission unexpectedly came to inspect our positions and mortars. The brigade command informed us that this UNPROFOR commission would come and inspect our positions in half an hour." Is it correct that this is a clarification that you made during the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you please just repeat the beginning of your question before this text that you read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure. Your Karadzic statement states: "Two or three days after the Markale incident in February 1994, an UNPROFOR commission unexpectedly came to inspect our positions and mortars." Do you need me to read further?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The team leader came then. I think he was a major, a Frenchman. And after arriving in our battalion, I mean, that's what was meant, he informed me that there was no firing from the defence area of our battalion. And he gave a gift both to me and to the commander, a belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll read on in your paragraph. But I just wanted to first confirm that this was a correction that you made during the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, just -- is it a correction or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Could you please take your earphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Stojanovic is speaking in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Weber, I noticed that on a page not shown to us, it's page 9, it says: "Additional information elicited on the 30th of November, 2012" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- "translated by the Karadzic Defence team." Whether it's a correction or not, and I take it, Mr. Stojanovic, that was one of your concerns, still may have to be established. And you presented it as: Is it true that you make this correction. I think you should inquire first into what this additional information -- what caused him to give this additional information. If that deals with the matter, then we have no problem with you speaking B/C/S, Mr. Stojanovic. Could the witness put on his earphones again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, could you please focus on paragraph 21 in this case, lest there be any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, how about this. I'll read out the full paragraph, paragraph 29, from your statement in the Karadzic case. And this is under a section entitled: "Additional Information," that you provided during that case. It says: "Two or three days after the Markale incident in February 1994, an UNPROFOR commission unexpectedly came to inspect our positions and mortars. The brigade command informed us ... this UNPROFOR commission would come and inspect our positions in half an hour. The UNPROFOR commission concluded that the mortars were not used for quite some time and that there were no traces of mortar use. In addition, they concluded that our crew did not even approach the mortars recently. A Russian member of the inspecting team measured and calculated the angles around the mortars and had a discussion with the rest of the team. One or two days later, a French officer came to our command, told us that they had concluded that our unit had not opened fire during the Markale incident, and gave his belt to the battalion commander, Gengo," it says, "as a present. The UNPROFOR team told us that we were the only unit in that area that they were interested in. We were also the only unit in that area." Is this the additional information that you provided in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning perhaps there was a mistake in translation or something like that, but 100 per cent sure it was the 6th when this mixed commission was held, the Serbs and the UNPROFOR. And then later on it's correct that this Frenchman came, this major. I think they belonged to the Foreign Legion, engineering. And I think he was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that this additional information that you provided in the Karadzic case appears inconsistent in terms of what you described in the Mladic statement; in particular, the timing. That it appears that you are describing similar events that occurred two or three days after the incident, and then you are also describing when the French officer came as being two days after that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the first check was carried out on the 6th. That's 100 per cent sure. It started at 10.00 and it went on for about three hours, a bit more than that, when the representatives of the Serbs were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not offer a report of your own related to this visit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not make a report because my chief of security was there and his deputy was there, and we together --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, did you have anything else to say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together we made this report, and I was there when it was coded and sent to Serb [as interpreted] because I could not send reports through my superiors, through the chief of security of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we give an opportunity for further examination. This French officer, did he come back a few days after the commission had visited you, as you said, on the 6th of February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in a few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He came back alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had a few officers with him and an interpreter, some girl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did they again go to the site where 120-millimetre mortars had been or did they just report the outcome of their earlier visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had not been there during the earlier visit. We went to both areas where the mortars were and we came back to the command. We did not stay there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. So if I understand you well, there was a visit on the 6th of February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this other one was two or three days -- well, I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now what were then the results, to the extent you know, of this first visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the first visit, this is my understanding of what the interpreter said to us when we asked, and our mortars were not used. That is 100 per cent sure. And there was no firing coming from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Interpreting from what language into what language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was from what language into what. You have answered the second part of my question, but what were the persons speaking whose words had to be translated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not very knowledgeable. I only speak Serbian. I've never spoken any other language, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm talking about his statement, what he said to us, I mean this interpreter. What he said to me, and to Pajic and Jakovljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether he was translating at that moment, or did he give his personal impressions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he was translating. After all, I don't know whether he had the right to present his personal views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- but you do not know whether he was translating --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just telling you what he said to us then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also describe this visit and you said: "They measured the azimuth." Could you explain to us what you exactly meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of these officer were measuring the azimuth, and they were doing this calculation in terms of the mortar and they were using a compass and so on, and they were writing things but I could not see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly by "azimuth"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the cardinal points. Things like that. Also the distance was measured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in terms of where the mortar was standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Distance from where to where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where the barrel was turned and then they measured the distance and this azimuth, and then they got their compasses out, orienting themselves. I know that they were trying to see where north/south was and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, what do you do you mean by they measured the azimuth? What do you understand to be the azimuth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point where we were. And then they were looking at where the mortars were because they had their own maps and they wouldn't allow us to look at those maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again, you say the azimuth, the point where you were. Does that mean, for example, the grid reference? The exact location? Is that what you mean by "azimuth"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Yes. Yes. The co-ordinate, the point, exactly where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what is often referred to as a grid reference. On a map you look at -- you are at 76 point -- that is what you call azimuth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you said they measured the distance. Distance between what and what? Because distance means --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were looking at the mortar itself, how the barrel was turned, in which direction. As far as I can remember, they were walking back and forth, taking a few steps back and forth. In terms of accent that was used, our comment was that this must have been a Russian, an expert for artillery. I mean, the accent of the speech that he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What language was he speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he spoke English, but his accent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you are telling us is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't sure. But that's an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us a minute ago that you are not that good in languages that you could tell us what people were speaking and when their words were translated. And I do understand your testimony to be now that you were able to hear what accent this officer had when he spoke English. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've told you after that he spoke English. I wasn't sure, but I understood his accent because he spoke differently from the others. He knew that language less than the other officers did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were able to hear that the others were speaking English, whereas a while ago when I asked you from what language --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you they spoke differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me take you back. A minute ago when I asked you from what language translation was made into your language, and then you said: "Well, I'm not that good at languages. I couldn't tell you." And now you're telling us that translation was made from English into Serbian. Have you any explanation why a minute ago you did not know what language they spoke that was translated to you and where you now seem to be certain about it being English and even being able to distinguish between the accent in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. However, I said that it was English. I said that I believed that it was English. I believe that the language spoken was English. I'm not sure. However, when he spoke, I realised that he spoke in a different accent than the others. I didn't understand what they were saying and not everything was interpreted for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to come back to the distance. The distance is to be measured between one point and another point. What distance did they measure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the mortar. That's where they took measurements and that's where they measured the distances. From one mortar to the next, the way they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the distance between one barrel and another barrel of this mortar --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let me -- and then I do understand they used a compass. Do you have any expert knowledge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any expert knowledge on mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they further explain why, as you heard from the interpreter, these could not have been the mortars that were used to fire projectiles that had landed on the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the truce was declared, everything was cleaned. Caps were put on the barrels so they would not go bad and the crews never approached those mortars. And it -- you could see with a naked eye that no mortar had been fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said caps were put on the barrels and you said the crews never approached those mortars, but that's not what this commission could establish, could they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could see on the spot there were no traces, nobody had been walking around them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These mortars had been there unattended and there were no footsteps, is that what you are saying as an explanation on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now just your personal opinion: Do you think that you could fire at the centre of the city of Sarajevo with those mortars as far as the location is concerned? I'm not asking whether they did or whether -- it's a 120-millimetre mortar, whether that can fire in such a way from that location so that it would be possible for a projectile to land on the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question fully. My personal opinion about 82 mortars [as interpreted], but this is 120-millimetre artillery. There is no way a shell could have landed there. There is a six-storey building and several three- or four-storey buildings. I used to come to that market every week for several years. I know the layout. And there were never so many people there at any one time that one round could have done so much damage. Historically, it was unknown. And in any case, that round could not have flown over that high building and could not have landed there. I really have my doubts about the whole thing. I believe that something had been planted. I am convinced. And the round was never fired from there. Either I or Gengo approved firing of the rounds when targets were defined according to range finders and those were only military targets. We did not have that many rounds so we were very careful how many we used; in other words, none of the crew were allowed or dared fire a round independently. I claim with full responsibility that that was not done from the positions of the 7th Battalion or from any of the positions of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the members of the commission that visited this site, whether they had expert knowledge about mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. Two of the officers were very familiar with artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the others were standing on the side and they were looking for a good spot from which they could define co-ordinates and the distance between the barrels and everything else, and they were the only ones who commented on the situation. The others didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were they the foreign officers or were they members --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were UNPROFOR members, foreigners. Our men did not have the right to approach the barrels. We were just observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was a mixed commission, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but they were the ones doing and we were the ones watching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said from their comments you understood that they were experts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You couldn't understand their comments, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but we heard it from the interpreter, providing that the interpretation was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you now describe the commission as UNPROFOR coming close to the location of the mortars; VRS Main Staff, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, staying at a distance, not even verifying their measurements or -- the UNPROFOR made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were all rather close to the barrels. When we came close to the mortars, we were standing near the trenches where our troops were deployed, and they were the ones who approached the mortars and took all the measurements. They did everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they share the measurements with you? Did they write it down and give it to you or to the Main Staff people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They marked those measurements in their own maps. As far as I know, they did not give us anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that commission didn't share anything they noted down at that moment with the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing was handed over. I believe that they promised that they would send everything through official channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they have kept that promise or did they break that promise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what happened. If they did send anything, it was sent to a superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: "I believe that they promised ..." You are not certain about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did promise, but I don't know whether they delivered on that promise. I think that they should have sent it to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is it, then, that a few days later another UNPROFOR group came to the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how was that composed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The head of that group was a French major. I believe that they belonged to the legion of foreigners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what did they do exactly during that visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We inspected both mortar positions, and on the way back, we also looked at Moscanica water source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did they measure anything? And if so, what did they measure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't measure anything. They just looked at the positions and then they returned. The whole visit was perhaps 10 minutes long. That's how long we stayed in the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And without having measured anything, I do understand you heard from the interpreter that the battalion had nothing to do with this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That major said it personally when we returned to the command. He gave us belts, to me and to my commander, while the interpreter interpreted for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they explain to you how just looking at the spot a bit, how they could establish that the battalion had got nothing to do with the incident, not having measured anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the statement was provided based on the previous investigations which were carried out both in Sarajevo and on the spot by the mortar positions. That was not his personal opinion. I believe that he just conveyed what his superiors thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was the first visit, did he tell that that had been part of the information on which his superiors had concluded that your battalion had got nothing to do with it, was that part of the information on which this conclusion was drawn? And I mean with the first visit, the mixed commission you told us about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way I understood him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Have the questions by -- first of all, Mr. Stojanovic, any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just check one thing. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Dzida. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you; questions put to you by the parties, questions put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm afraid we'll have to wait until the usher returns --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in order to have the witness escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can make use of this time. Last week the Chamber had made an inquiry about UNMO documents related to Lima V and I undertook to provide additional information this week. Unfortunately, I think I underestimated the size of the task and also the workload that we have, so I just want to inform the Chamber that we are working on it actively and it may take some more time. And as soon as we are able to provide fuller information to the Chamber, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you please -- could we agree that -- well, let's say that we hear from you somewhere in the next two weeks, would that be -- or would you need more time? The problem is if we have no agreed moment when we hear from you, there is always a risk that it slips out of our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I think Mr. Stojanovic undertook to provide that before the break. Could we set that as the date, the control date. But I think we will be able to provide something well in advance of that. So we would undertake to provide it at the same time as the Defence, but we'll endeavour to do it before then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, before the summer recess --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you say, yes. Okay. Then we'll hear from you before --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. We spoke to our witness who mentioned those reports, and he promised to send us information about those members of UNPROFOR with whom he spoke and then we will investigate further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may Ms. MacGregor and I please be excused. Do you mind if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Cvoro, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will call up a document in e-court. You will see it on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D1606.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there is some fear that it may be the wrong number and that what you really want to look at is 1D1601.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, perhaps Madam Registrar could show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke. I think I called for 1D1606.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we wonder whether that's really the document. Madam Registrar has a suspicion that you might want to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As always, Madam Registrar is right in these matters. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at that one and see whether you are happy to proceed. Madam Registrar, now is on the screen -- could you tell us, we have now a statement of -- which mentions the name of Mr. Cvoro. Could you tell us what number that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 1D1601.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And thank you to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. She assists the Defence in getting the right document on the screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvoro, I apologise. A little confusion occurred. You can see the document on the screen, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see the statement before and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it before and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvoro, do you recognise your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature and the date when I signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect what you stated before the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I said what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: My answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement as well as the associated documents. It's package 92 ter and we would like to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, first, good afternoon. Second, just one brief objection regarding the statement. I'm informed there is a translation inconsistency in paragraph 2 as to whether Mr. Cvoro was selected or elected to be president of the Executive Board, and I wonder if that could be remedied before it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the original, Mr. Lukic, and see whether it is about election or selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have witness statement, and we need page 2, paragraph 2, in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvoro, line 3.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I was elected to that position because I offered the best plan of work and I did not apply along party lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thank my learned friend for drawing my attention. I was not aware of this difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I take it, then, in the original it's also about elections --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it's a minor thing. Should we ask the revision of the translation or can we leave it to this as --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: With it having been corrected on the transcript, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the statement -- let me see. We have not yet had a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1601 receives number D492, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D492 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, could we go through the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Traldi, no objections against any of the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I understand there is only one that's not yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would only be 1D02022. Is that correct, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's our associated exhibit and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one and only. Madam Registrar, that document receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D02022 receives number D493, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D493 is admitted into evidence, and the other associated exhibit is already in evidence. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will read statement summary of this witness and it will be very short, even shorter than 35 lines. Witness Zdravko Cvoro was president of the Executive Board of Pale municipality. He will testify about the situation in the municipality of Pale in the relevant time-period. The municipality of Pale was overcome with trouble and distress of providing accommodations and humanitarian aid to refugees. Territorial Defence Staff controlled TO units and Crisis Staffs were formed automatically for emergency situations. The witness will testify how crimes committed against Serbs by Muslims in other areas made Muslim inhabitants of Pale fearful of retribution. The president of Pale municipality and the witness actively tried to get Bosnian Muslims to stay, and thus there was no forced expulsion of Muslims. That would be the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- questions for the witness, then please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Please can we have -- yes, we have paragraph 3 on our screen of Mr. Cvoro's statement, and I would have few questions in regard to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvoro, what was the position of municipal authorities vis-à-vis abandoned apartments? What was their number in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Since I was the president of the executive power, I ordered that each local commune and lower units had commissions set up. Those commissions would make lists of abandoned property. In Pale, there were over 2.000 weekend cottages because Pale was the lungs of Sarajevo. It is a small town which was a tourist destination. It lived off tourism. The climate and position of Pale lured many and inspired them to build their weekend cottages there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I may just ask a question. Mr. Cvoro, do you have -- by any chance know by whom these apartments had been abandoned? I'm talking about ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I'm talking about Muslim apartments and Muslim properties. And as for weekend cottages, they belonged to Muslims, Serbs, and Croats alike, because a weekend cottage is a holiday dwelling and many - including Muslims, Croats, and Serbs - were not present in those weekend cottages at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you manage to protect the property of those people who had abandoned the municipality of Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I take pride in the fact that all of the properties belonging to Muslims were mostly protected and preserved owing to the conscientious work of the commission. Before they took possession of an apartment, they listed all the abandoned properties. Whenever those houses were assigned to refugees and displaced persons, there was a record of the hand-over and they could only enter such properties under the control of municipal authorities. I'm not saying that there were no abuses. There were abuses, but we fought hard against those abuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did the first refugees arrive from in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: The first refugees arrived in Pale from the direction of Sarajevo. Those were Serbs. They had abandoned their territories, the places where they resided. I was among the first who abandoned their apartment and I arrived in Pale. When I was making a decision as to what to do, whether to stay or leave, I discussed the matter with my family and we decided that I had better make a mistake than to be sorry for the rest of my life. Many of the Serbs who lived in Sarajevo fled to Pale. And many Serbs also came from the depth of the territory across Serb territories, over mountains, and they arrived in Pale. One of such groups of refugees from Sarajevo consisted of the Serbian population from Pofalici. Under fire and facing skirmishes in the area, they fled, barefoot, without any belongings, they travelled across the mountain, and I don't know how they managed to get to Pale. I was informed about them during the night. I arrived there and we opened the school for them where they were accommodated for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Cvoro. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we continue, Mr. Cvoro?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were talking about the refugees from Pofalici and that you accommodated them at the school. Where did you accommodate refugees otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Well, a large number of them were received by the inhabitants of Pale; in particular, the elderly, the women, and the children. They were among the first. And then, as there was a great number of refugees arriving, we couldn't accommodate them all so we then forwarded some of them to Serbia. There were between five to ten buses with refugees that we sent on to Serbia. Sometimes even more. But the Municipal Assembly was in charge of the refugees. So they would first gather together in the big hall of the Municipal Assembly building, and we then brought them food and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm making a short pause because of interpretation. You said that five to ten buses left for Serbia, but in what time-period, as you didn't make any reference?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: During the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you prevent anyone from leaving?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: None except for the conscripts, the recruits who had to respond to call-ups for the mobilisation of the TO and the army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did people of other ethnicities - that is to say, the Muslims and the Croats - leave Pale at one point?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Do you mean generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When they left.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: They left at their own request.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the Muslims who were recruits? Could they leave?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: They stayed in Pale. They simply boycotted the call-ups for mobilisation. Those who personally requested to leave, I don't know, but it's possible that some even left for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the Croats who lived in Pale, did they leave Pale in great numbers?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Most of the Croats stayed in Pale and joined the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You have told us in your statement about the position to moving out, but we need another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2023, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will soon see it on the screen in front of you. It is a short document. We can see that it's dated the 12th of June, 1992. The president of the Municipal Assembly of Pale, Radislav Starcevic, addresses the secretary of the Pale SDS. So that the party would adopt a general position on the moving out of the non-Serbian population from the territory of Pale municipality --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of this document? Do you have a comment?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I'm aware of this document. Radislav Starcevic was the president of the Municipal Assembly in Pale. He was both a political figure and the president of the legislative powers because the Assembly is the highest legislative organ in the municipality, that is to say, of the local authorities. It's normal that he had to address somebody to have a basis for convening the Assembly as problems arose with the Muslims moving away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us briefly look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2023 receives number D494, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us look at another document, 1D2103, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see this document earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this document. It's a document from the police station in Pale and it followed from the Municipal Assembly decision from a session that was held on the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about this on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: It's a request for a departure and for changing the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean it was addressed to the SUP in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: No -- yes, addressed to the SUP in Pale, but it was the population, the Muslims from Pale who addressed this document to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see this document at the time or only during your preparations for testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Only during the proofing for my testimony in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you learn from conversation with the colleagues you worked with that such a request had been submitted and that there were requests submitted by Muslims who wanted to leave the territory of Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Well, I just said a while ago that the decision or the conclusion - I'm not sure how it was formulated - of the Assembly said that the records about the departure of Muslims would be kept by the public security station in Pale. On the basis of that conclusion, this request submitted by Muslims in which they asked to be allowed to depart followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2103 receives number D495, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if we could please have 1D2021, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document shows that SRNA, the Serbian press agency, reports on the 22nd of May about fighting in Renovica. Did you know at the time that fighting broke out, and did you know that the Muslim forces were being armed in the territory of the Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Well, the MUP, that is to say, the police of the municipality, was discharging its duties at the order of the relevant ministry. I as the president of the Executive Committee or at the time -- when was that? On the 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: May. Then I performed also the duty of the president of the Crisis Staff. I was informed of this activity, and I know that they went in the direction of Renovica in order to disarm the Muslims. On arrival, shots were fired at them. And I know that two policemen were killed, whereas five or six - I don't know exactly - were wounded. A conflict broke out in Renovica then and the conflict never ended, and certain lines were established on the ground in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is the neighbouring area to Renovica, what is there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: The local commune of Renovica comprises several villages, settlements, and so on, and behind it is the territory of Gorazde, which was held by the Muslim control throughout the war. So behind this local commune was Gorazde. Also, a part of the local commune of Praca was connected with the Muslim territory leading towards Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would tender this document, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2021 receives number D496, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, was the Muslim municipality of Pale already proclaimed or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I think not at the very beginning. But much later, the Muslim municipality of Pale was proclaimed, Pale Praca, and it exists to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to the Serbs from these two places, from Renovica and Praca?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: The Serbian population of Renovica immediately after the conflict of the police and -- I don't know how to call them, army or whoever they were, in Renovica, the rebels, the Muslims, the Serbs then left the territory of Renovica, even though there hadn't been many. 90 per cent of the population in the local community of Renovica were ethnic Muslims. As for Praca, those who were at the separation line also left their homes and withdrew towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for paragraph 16 of your statement, we don't have to show it on the screen, but let me just ask you something: How did the Muslims leave Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I can say that they left at their own requests, in an organised manner, without any problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they take anything with them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: They took away all the moveable property. They even took their motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think paragraph 16 deals with a specific group and so the witness may be somewhat confused about the questions he's being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- paragraph 16 at least starts with this truck -- trucks full of civilians coming from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can clarify. Thank you. Thank you for my learned friend's help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the organised departure of Muslims from Pale, was that the general manner in which they departed? I mean the Muslims from Pale.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Well, I said they left in an organised manner after the Municipal Assembly decision and after they submitted requests to depart from this territory, rather to change their place of residence. So we allowed them to do so. They did not all leave in one single day. It depended on the means of transportation that we had at our disposal and also security respects had to be taken into account, so they left in the direction of Sarajevo successively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now 1D2024. Could we just look at it briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see in front of us a conclusion dated the 14th of July, 1992, Executive Committee of the Pale municipality. Were you the chairman at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was the chairman then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Yes, of the Executive Committee. We were not satisfied with the commissions that were on the ground and made lists of moveable and immovable property. So we reacted and we adopted this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you actually want to achieve with this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: We wanted to revise the previous work of the commissions as we were not happy about it. There had been some unlawful acts, some property was misappropriated, and we then set up a revisory committee whose duty was to review the situation on the ground, to question the people who had made some abuses, and to take certain measures that were appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also see the last page of the document, please. That's page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says down here "Chairman Zdravko Cvoro," but I don't know whether this before it is "for"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Somebody signed that for me. But I remember it. I remember the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is not your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2024 receives number D497, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, tell us in whose weekend cottage you were in Pale and in what condition did you hand it over to the man who was the owner?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: I said in my statement and I said during the trial of Mr. Karadzic that I was in Hajrudin Somun's weekend cottage. He was either chef de cabinet or some advisor to Alija Izetbegovic. At the very outset - and he said that to me afterwards when we saw each other the war - he heard that his weekend cottage had been burned down, destroyed, that basically none of it was there anymore. After the war he came and, actually, he started working in the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, and some colleagues from Pale worked there too. He asked, "Do you know where my weekend cottage is and who is there now?" And they said that they knew and that a man, Zdravko Cvoro, was there. And he asked them for my telephone number and he contacted me. When he came to the weekend cottage, that was his property, of course, when he looked around he burst into tears. He said, "I cannot believe that everything is in its place." And he said, "Zdravko, you're a better man than I am." And I said, "Why, Hajrudin?" And he said, "You kept everything for me and I don't know if I would have kept things for you that way." And he said that he would thank me publicly through the media. He did that and, among other things, he said what he said and finally he said, "It's not only that he kept everything for me, I even found the last newspaper that I read in that weekend cottage." I'm not saying this for my own sake. I'm saying this on behalf of my fellow citizens who behaved in that way and in a similar way, preserving the property of the Muslims in Pale. All this property was returned, preserved, and further on they did whatever they chose to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what kind of condition did you find your apartment in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Totally destroyed, without anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvoro. That is all that I had for you for the time being.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Traldi, are you ready to start your cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Cvoro, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi, and I see you are looking already at him, is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvoro, before we turn to some of the specific events that are addressed in your statement, I want to ask very briefly: Have you spoken to anyone who has testified already in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know of anyone from this case that has anything to do with this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Have you spoken to Dragan Maletic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Dragan is my neighbour. He lives 200 metres away from me, and I haven't spoken to him at all about the case that has to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Setting aside the topic of any discussions you might have had with him for a moment, my question is just: Have you spoken to him since you've arrived in The Hague about any topic at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: Well, we talked about some of our private matters. He is carrying out this training. Then we talked about life and work in the area of Pale. As for his case or my case, they are not interlinked at all. I wasn't interested in his case and he wasn't interested in mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Have you spoken with anyone else who will be testifying in this case at some later time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you: You say he was not interested in my case, I was not interested in his case. What do you know about his case so as to say that you are not interested in it? What does he know about your case, I take it your testimony, that he showed to be not interested? How can you do that without talking about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was in the territory of Grbavica. He did not even live in Pale during the war. I assumed that, I mean, he was supposed to testify about that. Also, he was not in the territory of Pale. He is not familiar with that subject matter. We did not discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, not being interested in the other one's case suggests that you or he has expressed not being interested in it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just assume that he's not interested in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly. He never even asked me anything about that and I never asked him either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question to the witness. Sir, I'm asking you now -- I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said to one of the first questions of

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "No, I don't know of anyone from this case that has anything to do with this kind of thing. I don't know of anyone." And then you confirmed that you have met Mr. Maletic. Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, this is the way it is: I did not know Maletic at all until the Radovan Karadzic trial, and he's only 200 metres away from my house. And we never saw each other anywhere. We don't see each other in Pale. I'm a pensioner. He is an entrepreneur. He's working. We don't really have any contact as neighbours or any other kind of contacts so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I stop you. This was not my question. Where did you meet him? Did you meet him here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here in The Hague. That's where we met. He came before me. We met at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And at that time you knew that he is also here in The Hague in order to testify as a witness; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I saw him I assumed that he came to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And why did you say at the beginning: "No, I don't know of anyone from this case that has anything to do with this kind of thing," when you were asked if you have spoken to anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether that's what I said. I don't know anyone who is from my part. Well, that's what I meant. I don't know what I said. Or if I said it in that way. From my part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi asked you: "Have you spoken to anyone who has testified already in this case?" And then you said: "No, no. I don't know of anyone from this case ...," and so on. I leave it to that, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the same time it's a quarter past 2.00, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have just one more question on this general topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's, then, this hear this one question and the answer and then adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you signed your statement on the 10th of May of this year. Where were you when you signed your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: In Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I should have been more specific, but what building in Pale did you sign your statement in?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO
utterances.text: The public security centre in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was all I had on this topic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. We will adjourn for the day, but I would like to instruct you first that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever other way with whomever about your testimony. Testimony means testimony you have given today but it also applies to testimony still to be given next week, because we'd like to see you back on Monday morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume Monday, the 2nd of June, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning. But you're on your feet, Mr. Lukic, so I don't know for sure whether we adjourn already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you especially when you want to close the day, but you know that there is an issue about our fixed witness on Monday. So you instructed me to ask you whether it would be possible, since this witness has to leave on Tuesday. And I spoke with Mr. Cvoro. He was not happy with the solution but he accepted that if that gentleman has to leave, he'll wait for his testimony to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you -- apart from speaking to Mr. Cvoro, do you also have conversations with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has informed us and we have no objection. We are prepared to do Mr. Lalovic on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reasons are really so compelling that -- because the Chamber is also not very happy with interrupted witness statements. What is it that makes it so compelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next witness got a new job and he cannot -- he has been on that job only for 10 or 15 days, so he hardly got this short period of time because he just started to work, and he's in a danger to lose that job he was waiting for for more than a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber allows the change of the order of the appearing of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The present witness does not, at least not strongly object, Prosecution does not object. Madam Registrar, could the Victims and Witness Section inform Mr. Cvoro that he is not expected at 9.30 in the morning. Any chance that later in the morning he would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If possible, we would like to continue with Mr. Cvoro on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if Mr. Traldi would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, depends on Mr. Traldi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- if Mr. Lalovic is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we expect him to take less than a whole day in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd like that too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll start hearing the next witness Monday morning and then after that continue with Mr. Cvoro. The date is still the same, 2nd of June. Place is still the same, courtroom I. And the time is 9.30. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of June, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
